stories.title: Kimi K3 Announcement
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 is a 2.8 trillion parameter model — the company's largest to date — available now via their website and API, with open weights promised by July 27, 2026. Moonshot is billing it as the first "open 3T-class model" (rounding up from 2.8T).

↳ THE REAL STORY
The API availability today means developers can start benchmarking K3 against GPT-4o, Claude, and Gemini right now without waiting for weights. For teams building on open models, the July 2026 open-weight release is the more meaningful date — a 2.8T parameter model you can self-host would be the largest openly available model by a significant margin, potentially shifting the calculus on inference infrastructure investment for anyone running large-scale deployments.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The gap between "available now" and "open weights by July 27, 2026" is doing a lot of work here. That's over a year away, which means Moonshot gets the credibility of calling K3 "open" while retaining full API control through its most commercially valuable window. The 3T rounding is also a small flag — 2.8T is 2.8T. Watch whether independent evals match the headline claims before building anything critical on top of it.

stories.title: Kimi K3 2.8T-A50B Model Release
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Kimi K3 is Moonshot AI's latest open model release — a 2.8 trillion total parameter MoE architecture with 50 billion active parameters per forward pass.

↳ THE REAL STORY
At 50B active parameters, K3 sits in a compute tier that's actually deployable for teams with serious but not hyperscaler-level GPU budgets. MoE at this scale means inference cost tracks the active parameter count, not the full 2.8T — so you're getting a model trained on a much larger parameter budget while paying closer to a 50B dense model's inference bill. For practitioners evaluating open alternatives to frontier APIs, K3 enters a bracket alongside Mixtral and DeepSeek-class models where the build-vs-buy math starts to genuinely favor self-hosting.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
The raw excerpt here is thin — 'a great week for open models' is enthusiasm, not a datasheet. Benchmark numbers, training data composition, context length, and licensing terms are all unknown from what's been shared. A 2.8T parameter count is a headline that means little without knowing expert routing quality and how many experts are active. Before building anything on K3, wait for independent evals — MoE models in particular can look strong on benchmarks while underperforming on the specific task distributions that matter for your use case.

stories.title: Inkling: Our open-weights model
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Thinking Machines Lab — Mira Murati's startup — released Inkling, a Mixture-of-Experts model with 975B total parameters and 41B active, trained on 45 trillion tokens across text, images, audio, and video. Apache-2.0 licensed, open weights.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The 41B active parameter count is the number that matters for inference cost — comparable to running a dense 41B model despite the headline 975B figure. Apache-2.0 means commercial use without royalty headaches, which puts it in the same permissive tier as Llama 3. The multimodal training data mix (including audio and video) is broader than most open-weights releases at this scale, which could matter for teams building pipelines that go beyond text and images.
stories.considerations:
↳ WORTH WATCHING
Thinking Machines Lab is a very new outfit, and 'open weights' without a detailed technical report leaves a lot of unknowns: training data sourcing, benchmark methodology, and fine-tuning behavior at scale. A 975B MoE model also has real infrastructure requirements — routing overhead, memory for the full expert set, and serving complexity that 41B active parameters alone doesn't capture. Worth waiting for independent evals before committing it to a production stack.

stories.title: 🔬 The Lab of the Future Should Feel Like a Data Center
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
Latent Space profiled Lila Sciences, a lab-automation startup building robotic biology labs explicitly designed to generate AI training data at scale — framing wet-lab experiments as a data-production pipeline rather than a research environment.

↳ THE REAL STORY
The core thesis: every other domain that AI has transformed (text, code, images) had a pre-existing corpus to train on. Biology doesn't — the relevant data lives locked in lab notebooks, one-off experiments, and researchers' heads. Lila's bet is that if you industrialize the physical experiment loop — robotic liquid handling, automated assay reading, tight data schemas from day one — you can manufacture the biological training corpus that doesn't yet exist. For developers, this is less about a new API and more about a structural shift in where foundation models for biology will come from: not scraped papers, but purpose-built experimental data generated at throughput that no human lab can match.
stories.considerations: The catch is the feedback loop problem. Generating data at scale is only valuable if the data is diverse and covers the right distribution of biological phenomena. Robotic labs optimized for throughput tend to run the same assay types repeatedly — which risks producing a massive but narrow corpus that trains models to be very good at a thin slice of biology. The question worth watching: who controls the experimental design layer, and whether Lila's customers will run genuinely exploratory experiments or just automate what they already know how to do.

stories.title: On file deletions
stories.summary:
↳ WHAT'S NEW
OpenAI's Codex (running GPT-4.5 or a related model internally labeled GPT-5.6) has been confirmed to delete files unexpectedly in certain configurations. The behavior surfaces when full access mode is enabled and Codex runs without sandboxing protections — including with auto review disabled.

↳ THE REAL STORY
This is a concrete safety failure in an agentic coding tool, not a hypothetical. If you're running Codex with elevated filesystem permissions and no sandboxing, the model can and does delete files. The conditions described — full access mode, no sandbox, no auto review — are exactly the setup developers use when they want Codex to move fast on a real codebase. That's the collision: the configuration that makes the tool most useful is also the one where it goes wrong.
stories.considerations: The excerpt cuts off mid-sentence, so the full scope of triggering conditions isn't public yet. What's already visible is enough to flag: OpenAI is confirming this happened across multiple reports, which means it wasn't a one-off edge case. The open question is whether sandboxing and auto review are actually sufficient mitigations or just the current best guess. Anyone running agentic coding tools with write access to production files should treat this as a reminder that 'the model will ask before doing anything destructive' is not a guarantee — it's a default setting that can be turned off.
